title: "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo"

Random-walk MH proposes without consulting the target's local geometry. [**Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html) instead uses the gradient of the passage-level Student-t model log posterior to build a coordinated proposal in $(\mu,\log\sigma)$. The problem is random-walk behavior: many accepted short moves can still take a long time to cross a correlated target. A gradient supplies local information about which directions increase posterior density.

The target remains the conditional parameter distribution defined on the [posterior-distribution page](posterior-distributions.qmd); HMC changes the Monte Carlo transition, not that distribution. The [Monte Carlo page](monte-carlo-integration.qmd#expectations-as-integrals) explains why averages of target draws approximate posterior expectations.

What's going on mechanically? We will translate the log posterior into potential energy, add an auxiliary momentum with kinetic energy, and use leapfrog steps to move through the resulting system. Following one trajectory through the fitted passage model will then show both why the method can avoid random-walk behavior and why a fixed trajectory length leaves another problem to solve.

## Potential, kinetic, and total energy

Let $q$ denote unconstrained parameters and let $\rho$ be an auxiliary momentum. The potential energy is

$$
U(q)=-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y).
$$

For unit mass, draw $\rho\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ and define

$$
K(\rho)=\frac12\rho^\mathsf T\rho,
\qquad
H(q,\rho)=U(q)+K(\rho).
$$

Adding the momentum does not change the marginal posterior for $q$. It supplies a direction in which to construct a proposal.

Hamilton's equations are

$$
\frac{\mathrm dq}{\mathrm dt}=\rho,
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm d\rho}{\mathrm dt}=-\nabla U(q).
$$

The first changes position using momentum; the second changes momentum using the local posterior gradient.

In one dimension, imagine a ball moving across a valley whose height is $U(q)$. The slope $\nabla U(q)$ changes momentum, while momentum changes position. For the passage model, the $\mu$ component of the log-target gradient is

$$
\frac{\partial\log\widetilde f}{\partial\mu}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{55}
\frac{(\nu+1)(y_j-\mu)}{\nu\sigma^2+(y_j-\mu)^2}
-\frac{\mu}{s_\mu^2}.
$$

The summation is the Student-t likelihood contribution and the final term is the normal-prior contribution. In the code, this is the first element returned by `gradient_log_target()`.

## Leapfrog integration

For step size $\epsilon$, one leapfrog step is

$$
\rho_{t+\frac12}
=
\rho_t-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(q_t),
$$

$$
q_{t+1}=q_t+\epsilon\rho_{t+\frac12},
$$

$$
\rho_{t+1}
=
\rho_{t+\frac12}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla U(q_{t+1}).
$$

The half steps make the integrator reversible and volume preserving. Numerical integration changes the Hamiltonian slightly, so HMC accepts the endpoint with

$$
\alpha
=
\min\left\{1,
\exp[H(q,\rho)-H(q^*,\rho^*)]
\right\}.
$$

Thus one numerical step follows three visible operations: take half a momentum step using the gradient at $q_t$, take one position step using that updated momentum, then take the remaining half momentum step using the gradient at $q_{t+1}$. The code implements the two boundary half steps outside the loop and the intervening full momentum steps inside it.

## One trajectory through the passage-level Student-t model

The reference trajectory first whitens the grid posterior, then applies 12 leapfrog steps of size 0.20. Every potential and gradient evaluation still uses the observed 55-passage passage-level Student-t model. Whitening is a coordinate rescaling explained fully on the [mass-matrix page](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd#general-kinetic-energy): it makes the two posterior directions closer to comparable scales before a unit-mass trajectory is taken.

```{r}
#| label: provo-hmc-trajectory
library(ggplot2)

provo <- read.csv("data/provo/passage-summaries.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
y <- provo$noun_minus_verb_log_ffd
nu <- 4
prior_scale <- 2 * sd(y)
log_sum_exp <- function(x) { m <- max(x); m + log(sum(exp(x - m))) }
log_target <- function(eta) {
  mu <- eta[1]; sigma <- exp(eta[2])
  sum(dt((y - mu) / sigma, df = nu, log = TRUE) - log(sigma)) +
    dnorm(mu, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) +
    log(2) + dnorm(sigma, 0, prior_scale, log = TRUE) + eta[2]
}
gradient_log_target <- function(eta) {
  mu <- eta[1]; sigma <- exp(eta[2]); residual <- y - mu
  scaled_squared <- residual^2 / sigma^2
  c(
    sum((nu + 1) * residual / (nu * sigma^2 + residual^2)) -
      mu / prior_scale^2,
    sum(-1 + (nu + 1) * scaled_squared / (nu + scaled_squared)) -
      sigma^2 / prior_scale^2 + 1
  )
}
mode_fit <- optim(c(median(y), log(mad(y))),
                  function(eta) -log_target(eta),
                  gr = function(eta) -gradient_log_target(eta),
                  method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE,
                  control = list(reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000L))
local_sd <- sqrt(diag(solve(mode_fit$hessian)))
grid <- expand.grid(
  mu = seq(mode_fit$par[1] - 7 * local_sd[1],
           mode_fit$par[1] + 7 * local_sd[1], length.out = 321L),
  log_sigma = seq(mode_fit$par[2] - 7 * local_sd[2],
                  mode_fit$par[2] + 7 * local_sd[2], length.out = 321L)
)
grid$log_kernel <- apply(grid, 1, log_target)
grid$weight <- exp(grid$log_kernel - log_sum_exp(grid$log_kernel))
grid$sigma <- exp(grid$log_sigma)
grid_mean <- colSums(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")] * grid$weight)
centered <- sweep(as.matrix(grid[, c("mu", "log_sigma")]),
                  2, grid_mean, "-")
grid_covariance <- crossprod(centered * sqrt(grid$weight))
transform <- t(chol(grid_covariance))
inverse_transform <- solve(transform)

log_target_z <- function(z) log_target(grid_mean + drop(transform %*% z))
gradient_z <- function(z) {
  drop(t(transform) %*% gradient_log_target(grid_mean + drop(transform %*% z)))
}
record_state <- function(step, q, momentum) {
  eta <- grid_mean + drop(transform %*% q)
  potential <- -log_target_z(q)
  kinetic <- sum(momentum^2) / 2
  data.frame(step, mu = eta[1], sigma = exp(eta[2]),
             potential, kinetic, hamiltonian = potential + kinetic)
}

set.seed(2026101805)
epsilon <- .20
L <- 12L
q <- drop(inverse_transform %*% (mode_fit$par - grid_mean))
momentum <- rnorm(2)
path <- vector("list", L + 1L)
path[[1]] <- record_state(0L, q, momentum)
momentum <- momentum + .5 * epsilon * gradient_z(q)
for (step in seq_len(L)) {
  q <- q + epsilon * momentum
  if (step < L) momentum <- momentum + epsilon * gradient_z(q)
  else momentum <- momentum + .5 * epsilon * gradient_z(q)
  path[[step + 1L]] <- record_state(step, q, momentum)
}
path <- do.call(rbind, path)
energy_error <- tail(path$hamiltonian, 1) - path$hamiltonian[1]
acceptance_probability <- min(1, exp(-energy_error))

stopifnot(length(y) == 55L, abs(energy_error) < .001)
data.frame(step_size = epsilon, leapfrog_steps = L,
           energy_error, acceptance_probability)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-provo-hmc-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "A 12-step leapfrog path through the passage-level Student-t posterior. Contours come from the normalized grid; the two accent points are the trajectory endpoints."
grid$relative_density <- exp(grid$log_kernel - max(grid$log_kernel))
ggplot(grid, aes(mu, sigma, z = relative_density)) +
  geom_contour(color = "grey65", bins = 7, linewidth = .45) +
  geom_path(data = path, aes(mu, sigma), color = "#8B1A1A",
            linewidth = .75, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = path[c(1, nrow(path)), ], aes(mu, sigma),
             color = "#8B1A1A", size = 1.7, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Passage-level contrast (mu)",
       y = "Passage contrast scale (sigma)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The energy error is `r sprintf("%.6f", energy_error)` and the corresponding acceptance probability is `r sprintf("%.6f", acceptance_probability)`. These values assess this numerical trajectory; they are not probabilities that the linguistic model is true.

We choose $\epsilon=.20$ and $L=12$ because this combination produces a twelve-step trajectory with energy error below $.001$ for the present posterior. A smaller $\epsilon$ would usually improve numerical accuracy at greater computational cost, while changing $L$ would change how far the proposal travels. These values are neither estimated corpus properties nor settings that can be transferred to another posterior without checking its geometry.

## Recap and forward link

1. Potential energy is the negative log posterior kernel; momentum is an auxiliary proposal variable.
2. Gradients steer proposals along local target geometry.
3. Leapfrog's two half momentum steps make the numerical map reversible and volume preserving.
4. The accept--reject correction handles finite-step energy error.

The [mass-matrix page](mass-matrix-geometry.qmd#general-kinetic-energy) now develops the whitening transformation used in this demonstration.

## Check your understanding

1. Which energy contains the posterior kernel?
2. Why is momentum temporary?
3. Which two gradient evaluations enter a leapfrog step?
4. What does the final accept--reject step correct?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The potential energy $U(q)=-\log\widetilde f(q\mid\mathbf y)$ contains the posterior kernel. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Momentum is an auxiliary variable used to construct a proposal; integrating it out leaves the marginal posterior for $q$ unchanged. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A leapfrog step evaluates $\nabla U(q_t)$ before the position update and $\nabla U(q_{t+1})$ after it. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The final HMC accept--reject step corrects the small Hamiltonian error introduced by numerical leapfrog integration, preserving the target distribution. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
